evidence_quote: Lexus' streak of 11 consecutive years as the best-selling luxury marque in the U.S.
prompt: A mass-market carmaker known for reliable, economical small cars sells almost nothing above the mid-price segment, where European makers hold the luxury market. Proposal (1989): launch a separate luxury brand with its own dealer network and a flagship sedan engineered from scratch to match the European leaders on quality and refinement, priced well below them. Risks raised: buyers may not pay luxury prices to a company known for economy cars; a separate dealer network is costly; the European incumbents have decades of prestige; development has already cost heavily; a single flagship model at launch gives a thin line-up.

evidence_quote: between 2015 and 2018, Lucasfilm released several cinematic films, including critical and commercial successes like Episode VII: The Force Awakens and Rogue One
prompt: A large family entertainment company with theme parks, consumer products and a film studio is looking for franchises that can feed all of those businesses. Proposal (2012): buy a privately held film company that owns a famous space-fantasy franchise, whose founder is retiring, for about $4 billion in cash and stock, and produce a new trilogy of main films plus spin-off films. Risks raised: the franchise's most recent films drew mixed reviews; the founder's retirement removes its creative lead; the price is high against the company's current film output; fans may reject new entries; much of the franchise's merchandise value is already licensed out.

evidence_quote: Analysis of financial data suggests that the Osborne Effect did not materialize, with sales for Macs growing by 19% and 37% in the two quarters following March 2006.
prompt: A personal computer maker has used one processor family for over a decade; its chip supplier has not delivered processors cool and efficient enough for thin laptops, and that roadmap lags the dominant PC processor maker. Proposal (2005): move the whole computer line to the dominant PC processor architecture within about two years, shipping a translation layer so existing applications keep running. Risks raised: announcing early may freeze sales of current models; developers must rebuild their software; translated software will run slower; the brand's distinctiveness from ordinary PCs may weaken; the company's earlier processor transition was painful.

evidence_quote: As of 2020, third-party sales on Amazon accounted for 54% of paid units.
prompt: An online retailer sells books, music and a growing range of goods from its own inventory; it is not yet profitable. Proposal (2000): let independent sellers, including competitors, list new and used items on the same product pages next to its own offers, for a fee per sale. Risks raised: sellers will undercut its own prices on the same page; it has less control over outside sellers' service quality; used copies may cannibalize new sales; publishers and suppliers may object; customer trust in the site may suffer if sellers misbehave.

evidence_quote: in less than a decade, it became the first computer entertainment platform to ship over 100 million units.
prompt: A consumer electronics maker's planned CD add-on with the leading game console maker was cancelled by that partner. The home console market is held by two established game companies. Proposal (1994): launch its own CD-based console with 3D graphics, courting outside game developers with easier tools and cheaper disc manufacturing than cartridges. Risks raised: no experience as a console platform holder; the two incumbents have loyal customers and famous in-house game series; an incumbent's own 3D console launches around the same time; consoles sell at thin or negative hardware margins; outside developers must be won over.

evidence_quote: In 2022 alone, Jordan Brand brought in $5.1 billion to Nike.
prompt: A sportswear company that leads in running shoes is losing ground in basketball shoes. Proposal (1984): sign a rookie basketball player who has not yet played a professional game to a five-year endorsement deal worth far more than rivals offered, and build a signature shoe line around him, including colorways that break the league's uniform rules. Risks raised: the player is unproven as a professional; an injury could wipe out the deal's value; the league may fine him for wearing the shoe; the money is a large share of the marketing budget; signature shoes for a single player have rarely sold beyond a season.

evidence_quote: in February 2010, it was the largest music vendor in the world.
prompt: A computer maker whose portable music player is selling well faces widespread free file-sharing of music. Proposal (2003): open an online store selling individual songs for 99 cents each with light copy protection, after licensing catalogs from all major record labels. Risks raised: free file-sharing is everywhere; labels may withdraw their licenses; 99 cents leaves little margin after label payments; the store at first works only on the company's own computers; rivals are backing music subscriptions instead of per-song sales.

evidence_quote: The Walkman has sold more than 250 million units worldwide.
prompt: An electronics maker sells tape recorders and hi-fi equipment. Proposal (1979): sell a small stereo cassette player with lightweight headphones, no speaker and no recording function, at a price aimed at young people. Risks raised: dealers and staff doubt a tape machine that cannot record; listening alone through headphones may seem antisocial; no market research shows demand; it is built from existing parts that competitors could copy; the first production run must be large to reach the price.

evidence_quote: the Super Cub is the most produced motor vehicle* in history.
prompt: A Japanese motorcycle maker leads its home market with a small, easy-to-ride 50cc step-through motorcycle. In the United States motorcycles are large machines with a rough image, and the market is small. Proposal (1959): open a US subsidiary and sell the small step-through to commuters and students, including through sporting-goods and other non-motorcycle shops. Risks raised: Americans favor big motorcycles; the brand is unknown there; the company's larger models may not hold up to long runs at US highway speeds; setting up abroad ties up scarce foreign currency.

evidence_quote: Within two years, they became Apple's most popular accessory.
prompt: A phone maker is removing the headphone jack from its new phone. Proposal (2016): launch fully wireless earbuds with a charging case at $159, using its own wireless chip for automatic pairing with its devices. Risks raised: the earbuds look odd and may be ridiculed; they are easy to lose; $159 is high against the free wired earphones in the box; battery life is about five hours; removing the jack may anger customers.

evidence_quote: over 100 million Alexa-enabled devices had been sold.
prompt: An online retailer's first smartphone has just sold poorly. Proposal (2014): launch a cylindrical home speaker with an always-listening voice assistant that plays music, answers questions and adds items to shopping lists, at $199 ($99 for paying members at first), sold by invitation at first. Risks raised: customers may not accept an always-on microphone at home; voice recognition often fails; no product category like it exists; the company's last hardware launch went badly; phone-based assistants already exist.

evidence_quote: it helped revitalize the American gaming industry following the 1983 crash
prompt: The North American home video game market collapsed in 1983; retailers are clearing stock and many see video games as a passed fad. A Japanese toy and game company has a cartridge console that leads its home market. Proposal (1985): launch it in North America styled as an entertainment system, bundled with a light gun and a toy robot rather than sold as a game console, with a lockout chip that limits which outside companies may publish games, and a promise to take back unsold stock from retailers. Risks raised: retailers are refusing to stock video games; the company has no console track record outside Japan; cheap home computers also play games; publishing limits may anger developers; the take-back promise exposes it to large returns.

evidence_quote: The highest-selling line of minivans worldwide, Chrysler produced the 15 millionth example of the model line in 2019.
prompt: A carmaker was recently saved from collapse by a government loan guarantee. Families buy station wagons or full-size vans. Proposal (1983): launch a new front-wheel-drive van sized to fit in a home garage and drive like a car, built on its existing compact-car platform, with a converted factory. Risks raised: no such vehicle category exists; the company has little cash; buyers may see it as a commercial van; rivals could copy it; reusing a compact-car platform may limit space.

evidence_quote: More than one million MX-5s have been sold, making it the best-selling two-seat convertible sports car in history.
prompt: Small British two-seat roadsters have disappeared from the market, and mass-market makers regard open two-seaters as a dead niche. Proposal (1989): a mid-size carmaker launches an affordable, lightweight, front-engine, rear-drive two-seat convertible inspired by those roadsters. Risks raised: the segment has shrunk for years; two seats limit buyers; safety rules make convertibles costly; the company has no sports-car heritage in this class; sales may fade once early enthusiasts have bought.

evidence_quote: Advertising sales goals were not met and in 2016 Yahoo wrote down $712 million of Tumblr's value.
prompt: A web portal losing relevance among young users wants a younger audience. Proposal (2013): buy a fast-growing blogging platform popular with young people, with little revenue, for $1.1 billion in cash, keep it independent and grow advertising on it. Risks raised: the platform's users dislike ads; some of its content is adult and hard to sell to advertisers; the portal has struggled to integrate past acquisitions; the price is high against revenue; the founder may leave.

evidence_quote: After only 48 days on the market, Microsoft discontinued the Kin line on June 30, 2010
prompt: A software company with a large phone-software business is preparing a new phone platform. A separate social-phone project for young people, built by a team from an acquisition, has been delayed by a switch of its underlying software. Proposal (2010): launch two social-networking phones for young people through one carrier, requiring a full smartphone data plan, with no app store and no games. Risks raised: target buyers are price-sensitive; the data plan costs as much as a smartphone's; the company's main new phone platform launches later the same year; there are no third-party apps; the two teams have a history of internal conflict.

evidence_quote: Sales of the Newton were well below Apple's expectations
prompt: A computer maker wants to lead a new category of handheld computers. Proposal (1993): launch a pen-based personal digital assistant at about $700 with handwriting recognition as its main input, after heavy publicity by the chief executive. Risks raised: handwriting recognition is unreliable in testing; the price is high; it is too big for a pocket; there is little software; the category is unproven.

evidence_quote: The Virtual Boy was panned by critics and became a commercial failure despite repeated price cuts.
prompt: A leading game company wants a new product between its handheld and home-console generations. Proposal (1995): launch a tabletop stereoscopic 3D console with red monochrome displays viewed through an eyepiece, at about $180. Risks raised: red-on-black visuals only; it is neither portable nor comfortable to use; some users may get eye strain or headaches; few games at launch; the company's next home console is due within two years.

evidence_quote: The company failed to earn revenue sufficient to service the debt associated with building out the constellation and Iridium went bankrupt
prompt: A company has spent about $5 billion, much of it borrowed, building a 66-satellite network for worldwide mobile phone service. Proposal (1998): launch commercial service with handsets at about $3,000 and calls at several dollars a minute, aimed at international business travelers. Risks raised: ground cellular networks are spreading fast; handsets are bulky and work poorly indoors; the price limits the market; debt payments require fast subscriber growth; sales channels are not ready.

evidence_quote: American sales did not live up to early expectations mainly due to customers' lack of interest in a mid-calorie soda
prompt: The largest cola maker sees low-carb diets hurting its sugar sodas while diet cola grows. Proposal (2004): launch a mid-calorie cola with half the sugar and carbohydrates, priced at a premium, with a large campaign aimed at young men. Risks raised: people who want fewer calories already buy the diet version; a half-sugar drink may satisfy neither group; the premium price may deter trial; a rival is launching a similar drink; the low-carb trend may be a fad.

evidence_quote: Many of the 700,000 units shipped to retailers allegedly remained on the shelves for months, prompting BlackBerry to introduce dramatic price reductions in November 2011 to increase sales.
prompt: A smartphone maker that leads in business email faces a fast-growing touchscreen tablet from a rival. Proposal (2011): launch a 7-inch tablet on a new operating system it bought, initially without built-in email, calendar or contacts apps unless paired with the company's phone. Risks raised: the rival tablet has a large app store; shipping without built-in email undercuts the business pitch; the new operating system is untested; the price matches the rival's larger tablet; developers may not commit.

evidence_quote: with only 3 million units sold in its two years, the N-Gage was a commercial failure
prompt: The largest mobile phone maker wants a share of the handheld game market led by a dedicated game company. Proposal (2003): launch a phone that doubles as a handheld game console, at about $300, with games on memory cards. Risks raised: changing a game card means removing the battery; it is awkward to hold for calls; the market leader has a huge game library; the price is far above the leader's handheld; game publishers are uncommitted.

evidence_quote: By 2003, the company had sold 6,000 units
prompt: A well-known inventor's company has built a self-balancing two-wheeled personal transporter, backed by prominent investors and heavy publicity. Proposal (2001): launch it at about $5,000 with a factory sized for about 40,000 units a year. Risks raised: its legal status on sidewalks and roads is unclear; the price is high; uses beyond institutional buyers are unproven; riders may feel conspicuous; it cannot carry much.

evidence_quote: Expectations created for the car during the run up to its production were out of proportion with realised sales.
prompt: An Indian carmaker has developed a basic four-seat car to move families from scooters to cars. Proposal (2008): launch it at about 100,000 rupees (about $2,500), marketed as the cheapest car in the world, from a new dedicated factory with high volume targets. Risks raised: the factory site faces protests from farmers over land; cost cutting may raise doubts about safety and quality; buyers may not want a car known as the cheapest; scooters and used cars are cheaper alternatives.

evidence_quote: GM forecast sales of up to 75,000 Azteks per year and needed to produce 30,000 annually to break even.
prompt: A large carmaker's mid-market division wants a youthful crossover between a minivan and an SUV. Proposal (2001): launch a minivan-based crossover with a distinctive angular body and camping options such as a tent and cooler, priced in the mid-$20,000s, needing about 30,000 sales a year to break even. Risks raised: early customer clinics rated the styling poorly; it sits on an aging minivan platform; cost cuts during development compromised the design; it has no real off-road ability.

evidence_quote: Upon release, Microsoft Bob was criticized in the media and did not gain wide acceptance with users, which resulted in its discontinuation.
prompt: A software company leads PC operating systems; many new home users find computers hard to use. Proposal (1995): sell a home-user shell in which programs appear as rooms of a cartoon house with cartoon guides, at about $100, requiring a high-end PC. Risks raised: it needs more memory than most home PCs have; experienced users may find it patronizing; a major new operating-system release with a new interface is coming within months; few third-party add-ons.

evidence_quote: The Saturn was initially successful in Japan but not in the United States, where it was hindered by a surprise May 1995 launch, four months before its scheduled release date.
prompt: A game company's 32-bit console is scheduled for a US launch in September 1995, when a new competitor also arrives. Proposal (1995): launch four months early, in May, announced at a trade show, shipping only to a few retailers at $399 with few games ready. Risks raised: retailers left out may retaliate; few games will be available; the price is $100 above the rival's announced price; developers did not plan for the early date; the machine is hard to program for 3D.

evidence_quote: the Lisa platform failed to achieve sales volumes comparable to the much less expensive Macintosh
prompt: A personal computer maker has built a business computer with a graphical interface and a mouse. Proposal (1983): launch it at about $10,000 for office workers. Risks raised: the price is several times that of leading business PCs; it runs slowly; there is little third-party software; a cheaper machine with a similar interface is being developed inside the same company.
